Conic sections. The curves produced when a plane intersects a double cone at various angles. The four fundamental types—circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola—form the backbone of analytic geometry.

The four types are determined by the angle at which the cutting plane meets the cone's surface. A circle results when the plane is perpendicular to the cone's axis. An ellipse results when the plane is tilted but does not intersect the cone's base. A parabola results when the plane is parallel to one of the cone's generators, the slanting lines on its surface. A hyperbola results when the plane cuts through both nappes, the two parts, of the double cone.

All conic sections can be expressed in the general form A x squared plus B x y plus C y squared plus D x plus E y plus F equals zero. The discriminant B squared minus four A C determines which type. The ancient Greeks, especially Apollonius, classified conics. The Renaissance recovered and extended their study.

The four types relate closely through eccentricity. A circle has zero eccentricity. An ellipse has eccentricity between zero and one. A parabola has eccentricity exactly one, serving as the transition between ellipse and hyperbola. A hyperbola has eccentricity greater than one.
